works.title: Multimodal Task Attention Residual Reinforcement Learning: Advancing Robotic Assembly in Unstructured Environment_supp1-3547647.mp4
Learning Contact-Rich Assembly Skills Using Residual Admittance Policy
works.venue: 2021 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)

works.abstract: <jats:p>Driven by demands for assembly quality and efficiency, robotic assembly has become a cornerstone of autonomous industrial systems. However, contact-rich assembly tasks are constrained by challenges in reliability, data efficiency, and generalization, making conventional position control insufficient for stability and robustness in real-world autonomous production lines. Although compliant control, visuo-tactile sensor fusion, and imitation learning have emerged as enablers of adaptive robotic behavior, the existing literature lacks a systematic review encompassing task modeling, policy generalization, and standardized evaluation. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the imitation learning application framework for robotic assembly, organized around three core dimensions: reliability, efficiency, and adaptability, which constitute fundamental requirements for industrial deployment: predictable physical interaction, cost-effective, and robust adaptation to product variants and environmental changes. To establish a foundation for understanding data-driven capabilities and limitations, we describe the physical components of an assembly system, including demonstration modalities, hardware topology, and multimodal perception. Building on this, we trace algorithmic evolution from structured movement primitives to generative policies, proposing a selection methodology to guide integrated manufacturing deployment. Furthermore, this review surveys prevailing benchmarks and data ecosystems; to overcome the limitations of current evaluation metrics that prioritize outcomes over processes, we propose a standardized evaluation protocol. This protocol enables unified quantitative diagnostics across four dimensions: task accomplishment, contact quality, generalization robustness, and system resilience. Finally, the bottlenecks impeding the transition of robotic assembly from lab to autonomous industrial deployment are identified, followed by a discussion of prospective research frontiers.</jats:p>
works.title: Toward Autonomous Contact-Rich Robotic Assembly: A Review of Imitation Learning
